Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Elena was twenty-four when she was taken to a windowless concrete room. The guards had fastened thick canvas restraints across her wrists and ankles, binding her to a steel chair so she could not shift, reach the door, or find any way out. She had been left there for hours in the crushing silence, feeling the absolute certainty that there was no option but to remain. When the door finally opened, a female guard in a dark uniform stepped inside, her voice cold and deliberate as she paced the narrow floor. Over the following days, Elena was forced to watch other captives being led past the bars, their faces marked by fresh bruises and bleeding cuts. The woman who administered the shocks was always female, her hands steady, her expression unreadable. Elena learned to brace herself the moment she heard women’s footsteps or saw a tear in someone’s sleeve, because that was how the violence always began. The habits began quietly. When Elena walked past a coworker’s arm and saw a fresh bandage wrapping his forearm, her pulse jumped, and she immediately began testing every deadbolt on her apartment door. Seeing a wound was enough to set off a chain of compulsive checking, and she found herself pacing the entryway for an hour, pressing her palm against the wood, waiting until the click of the latch felt absolute. She also started waking at 3 a.m., her breath shallow, convinced she had to verify the windows were sealed before she could let herself drift back into exhaustion. Her body never learned that the danger had passed; it only knew to stand guard. That fleeting sense that she could never predict who might harm her added only a quiet hum to the constant checking, never commanding it but lingering at the edges. As the weeks bled into months, Elena’s mind began to rewrite what happened to her. She stopped trying to hold the images because they would arrive like a sudden weight in her chest, so overwhelming that she had to drop whatever she was doing and press her forehead against the wall until the wave passed. The memories felt detached, as if they belonged to a stranger who had lived a different life, and this distance made her question her own reliability. She had come to believe she was fundamentally altered, permanently damaged by what she had survived, and that conviction made the past feel even more alien. The shame that accompanied each recall only reinforced her self-doubt, convincing her that she could never trust that she would react correctly if violence returned. Her work as an HVAC technician once involved steady climbs through attics and tight service tunnels, but now the narrow crawl spaces triggered a paralyzing memory of the restraints. Whenever she dropped into a dark utility shaft, the shame of the past rushed back, so overwhelming that she had to stop, sit on the concrete, and press her palms flat against her knees until the panic receded. That overwhelming recall did not stay contained; it spiked her alertness immediately, making her jumpy and hyper-aware of every creak in the building. Because her mind could no longer separate the remembered trauma from the present room, she began scanning for visible injuries on herself and others, convinced she had permanently changed for the worse. That conviction made her doubt her own judgment, and the self-doubt pushed her to retreat from being alone with female clients or crew members. The constant checking of door locks followed, a relentless need to verify safety, which in turn cemented her belief that her nervous system was broken beyond repair. Her heightened startle response and waking alertness only magnified her sensitivity to specific cues, making the presence of women or visible wounds feel immediately dangerous. Elena has finally booked a clinical intake because the avoiding has cost her a long-term contract with a regional contractor, and her apartment has become a perimeter she no longer wants to defend alone. She sits on the edge of the exam chair, her hands resting heavily on her thighs, and admits that she is exhausted by the constant need to verify the doors are secure. What she hopes for is not to erase the past, but to learn how to stand in a room without feeling like she is already trapped. What she fears most is that the damage is irreversible, that the part of her that once could fix broken systems is gone, and that she will never trust her own instincts again.
